No centroiding, smoothing, filtering, or peak-picking options were enabled in msConvert; it was configured strictly for lossless profile-data preservation and format interoperability. The conversion preserved full-scan MS1 (m/z 100–1000) and data-dependent MS2 spectra at specified resolutions (70,000 at m/z 200 for MS1; 17,500 at m/z 200 for MS2). Final outputs are exported as comma-separated value (*.csv) files containing centroided m/z–intensity pairs along with associated DQS values and parameter uncertainties. Supplementary implementation details for TOF-MS (using Bi-Gaussian modeling) and validation datasets (e.g., Samanipour et al., 2021 [23]) are provided in the SI.'}

Key procedural steps include: (1) Storing numerical data (e.g., m/z values, intensities, chromatogram start times) in native HDF5 datasets (e.g., 'spectrum_MS_1000514_double', 'spectrum_MS_1000515_float') instead of Base64-encoded XML <binary> tags; (2) Embedding full mzML XML metadata inside an HDF5 character array dataset named 'mzMLb', modified such that <binary> tags contain only attributes specifying the HDF5 dataset name and byte offset (not embedded binary data); (3) Replacing mzML index structures (<indexed mzML>) with native HDF5 one-dimensional 64-bit integer arrays ('mzML_spectrumIndex', 'mzML_chromatogramIndex'); (4) Applying a lossy but highly controlled coding scheme combining three components: (a) mantissa bit truncation (e.g., reducing double-precision 52-bit mantissa to fewer bits, conservatively capped at ≤21 bits removed to maintain <2×10⁻⁹ relative error for m/z and <2×10⁻⁴ for intensities), (b) HDF5 shuffle filter to rearrange bytes for improved zero-run compressibility, and (c) 'mzLinear' linear extrapolation predictor — storing only the residual error Δh = yₙ₊₂ − (2yₙ₊₁ − yₙ) — optimized for quadratic m/z relationships (e.g., time-of-flight MS); (5) Integrating optional compression backends: zlib (for high-ratio lossless/lossy compression) and BLOSC with LZ4HC (for ultra-fast, low-overhead compression targeting speed-critical use cases); (6) Empirically optimizing HDF5 chunk size across 16 KB to 2048 KB ranges, identifying 1024 KB as the default balancing compression ratio, write speed, and random read latency; (7) Validating downstream impact via Mascot PSM search and protein inference workflows on AgilentQToF and QExactive datasets, comparing peptide/protein lists, E-values, and score deviations against uncompressed originals and Numpress-compressed controls."}

The workflow comprises: (1) Input of profile-mode *.mzXML spectra; (2) Peak isolation by detecting zero-intensity regions (for resolved peaks) and valley points (for splitting overlapping profiles, with valley points assigned to both adjacent peaks); (3) Log-transformation of each isolated Gaussian-shaped peak profile to linearize the Gaussian model Î(x) = Î₀·exp[−(x−x̂₀)²/(2σ̂²)] into a second-order polynomial ln(Î(x)) = β̂₀ + β̂₁x + β̂₂x²; (4) Weighted linear regression using sparse matrix algebra, where weights wᵢ = Iᵢ / ΣIᵢ² (intensity-squared weighting optimized for Orbitrap-MS); (5) Estimation of Gaussian parameters (centroid x̂₀, width σ̂, height Î₀, area Â) via closed-form solutions (Eqs. 3–6); (6) Calculation of regression standard errors via the variance–covariance matrix s̆²(β) = MSE·(XᵀWX)⁻¹, with MSE computed from weighted residuals (Eq. 13); (7) Derivation of the Data Quality Score (DQS) = 1 − erf(ΔÂ/Â), where ΔÂ is propagated from uncertainties in Î₀ and σ̂ using error propagation (Eq. 11); (8) Filtering out poor fits based on two criteria: β̂₂ < 0 (ensuring real-valued σ̂) and minimum 4 data points per peak (to ensure ≥1 degree of freedom); (9) Export of final centroided results (m/z–intensity pairs with DQS) to *.csv. The algorithm avoids deconvolution for overlapping peaks to prevent computationally prohibitive non-linear regression, instead relying on valley-based splitting. A Bi-Gaussian extension for TOF-MS is described in the supplementary material but was not part of the primary implementation shown in the main text.'}

Isolation windows were set to ±1.00 m/z (AB SCIEX), ±1.25 m/z (Thermo), and ±1.50 m/z (Agilent, Waters). For Waters data, subscan summation was first performed within msConvert using a custom algorithm that summed intensities at identical m/z values across MS/MS spectra sharing the same precursor (within 0.05 m/z and 30 s retention time tolerance, matching Mascot Distiller settings). Vendor libraries were also accessed through msConvert: Thermo and Agilent peak-picking and charge determination libraries were used for comparative analysis (though neither includes deisotoping, so ProteoWizard’s Poisson deisotoper was subsequently applied). (2) Precursor charge determination using Turbocharger, which first runs CantWaiT on survey scans surrounding each MS/MS spectrum (two preceding for Thermo/Waters; one preceding + one following for AB SCIEX/Agilent), then builds isotopic chains with interpeak spacing = m_neutron/q ± 0.06 m/z (m_neutron = 1.00335 Da), scores chains using three metrics—(i) m/z spacing fidelity (sum of squared errors vs. simulated null distribution, converted to p-value), (ii) relative intensity distribution (Kullback–Leibler divergence vs. Poisson isotopic model, p-value from 10,000 simulations), and (iii) intensity rank-sum (p-value from combinatorial rank distribution)—then sums ranks across metrics and applies post-hoc correction (selects longer chain if top-8 contains same peaks plus leading peak and passes p < 0.30 relative intensity criterion). {'sample_description': 'The sample used in the research consists of centroided liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC/MS) data in the open-source .mzML format across N_tot samples in a cohort. Each sample file contains data points x = (rt, m/z, u), where rt is retention time, m/z is mass-to-charge ratio, and u is intensity. An individual peak is defined as a subset of data points from a single sample with nearly identical m/z values (corresponding to the same ion) and intensities forming a bell-shaped profile along the rt axis. Peaks corresponding to the same underlying ion across multiple samples constitute a peak group (or feature), characterized by similar shapes, nearly equal m/z values (with small variations due to machine precision), and non-linear rt drift across samples.', 'XCMS_configuration_description': '', 'process_procedure_description': 'The method employs the mzLearn algorithm—a software tool specifically designed for LC/MS feature detection and alignment—not XCMS. The procedure comprises six sequential stages: (A) Patch creation: Each sample is partitioned into non-overlapping, dynamically resized bounding boxes (patches) enclosing potential peaks; coarse patching uses MZ_coarse = 2 × mz_tol × MZ_max and RT_coarse = RT_max / 5; dynamic resizing adapts patch boundaries using distance thresholds D_rt = μ_drt + 0.1σ_drt and D_mz = μ_dmz + 0.1σ_dmz computed from successive point distances along rt and m/z axes; noisy patches are removed via autocorrelation filtering with an initial threshold Tac(0) = 0.5, refined iteratively to the 5th percentile of per-peak autocorrelation scores after Stage-1 and Stage-2 pin discovery. (B) Cross-sample patch alignment: Reference patch X_p from sample k is cross-correlated with candidate bounding boxes X′ in sample k′, whose rt bounds are initially set to [rt_min + lbd, rt_max + ubd] with lbd = −RT_max/50 and ubd = RT_max/50; rt axes are binned at Δ = μ_drt/10, with intensity averaging for multi-point bins and interpolation (or min-intensity imputation when drt > D_rt) for empty bins; alignment function AL(X_p, X′, d) = w_μd,σd[d] ⋅ (F_ΔX_p ⋆ F_ΔX′)[d] is maximized over rt-displacement d to determine optimal alignment d*, yielding aligned patch-group pairs {X_p^k, X_p^k′}. (C) rt-drift estimation and re-alignment: A learned rt-drift map is constructed to estimate sample-wise rt drift (μ_d) and uncertainty (σ_d); the expected drift function w_μd,σd[d] is updated to be 1 within the 2σ_d neighborhood of μ_d and decay to 0 beyond it, refining the alignment function in subsequent iterations. (D) Peak extraction: Peaks are extracted from aligned correlated-patch groups using shape-aware criteria. (E) Peak group refinement: Candidate peak groups are improved using updated parameters and the refined rt-drift map in an iterative learning loop (three total iterations). (F) Intensity drift correction: An intensity drift map is estimated and applied to normalize feature intensities across samples, correcting for instrument-induced intensity drifts. The final output is a two-dimensional feature table where rows represent features (peak groups) and columns represent normalized intensities across N_p samples.'}

Input preparation requires users to supply feature tables (csv/tsv format) containing m/z, retention time, and intensity per LC–MS run; raw files (if using profile-based alignment) must be converted to mzML (via MSConvert) or aird (via AirdPro) format. Retention time alignment is performed using two built-in methods: (i) RANSAC (RANdom SAmple Consensus)—a feature-based, iterative, outlier-robust method that fits linear or nonlinear models by selecting random subsets, classifying inliers/outliers based on model consistency, and selecting the model with maximum inliers; default setting uses linear RANSAC due to speed, stability, and no raw file dependency; (ii) OBI-Warp—an open-source Python implementation (first of its kind) of Ordered Bijective Interpolated Warping, which extends dynamic time warping (DTW) to compute optimal bijective warping functions between LC–MS profiles, followed by piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation for smoothness; previously validated in XCMS (OBI-Warp) and MZmine2 (RANSAC). Feature matching proceeds in three stages: (1) Graph building—features across all runs are superimposed in a shared m/z–retention time coordinate system; neighborhoods are searched using user-defined m/z tolerance (Δm/z) and retention time tolerance (ΔRT); an undirected relation graph is constructed where nodes represent features and edges represent potential correspondences; edge weights are computed as weighted sum: (1/3) × (|Δm/z|/m/z_tolerance + |ΔRT|/RT_tolerance + 1 − min(normed_area)/max(normed_area)), where normed_area = feature_intensity / max_intensity_in_component_per_run. (2) Graph splitting—relation graph is decomposed into maximal connected components (each representing candidate analyte groups), treated as independent multipartite subgraphs where nodes from the same run belong to the same partite and edges only connect nodes from different runs. (3) Assignment solving—the feature matching problem is formulated as an unbalanced multidimensional assignment problem (MAP) on each multipartite component: each solution γ contains p matchings (p = max(n₁,…,nₘ)+1), each matching γⱼ is a unique M-partite linkage Lᵢ₁…ᵢₘ = {fᵢ₁¹,…,fᵢₘᴹ} including optional placeholder nodes fₙₖᵏ indicating unmatched runs; constraints ensure node uniqueness, non-overlap of non-placeholder nodes, and full coverage of all features. Matching cost C(γⱼ) comprises: distribution cost (total weight of minimum spanning tree of the subgraph induced by γⱼ), connectivity cost (w_c × N_c, where N_c = number of connected subgraphs in induced subgraph), missing node cost (w_p × N_p, where N_p = number of placeholder nodes), and full-match bonus (−b for fully connected matchings without placeholders); all penalty/bonus parameters (w_c, w_p, b) are pre-optimized and non-adjustable. Three solvers are provided: (i) Gurobi solver—converts MAP to integer linear programming and uses Gurobi optimizer for global optimum; (ii) Greedy solver—iteratively selects minimum-cost matching, marks matched features as unavailable (infinite cost), and builds solution incrementally; (iii) VLSNS solver—variable-length stochastic neighborhood search (details not fully shown in excerpt but implied as a heuristic alternative).'}

No further configuration parameters (e.g., noise threshold, minimum peak height, chromatographic alignment settings, or deconvolution parameters) are explicitly described in the text for MZmine.", 'process_procedure_description': "The Automated Target Screening (ATS) workflow is implemented as an R package (R v4.1.3) available on GitHub. It consists of six main steps executed via five core functions: (A) EIC generation and peak identification/integration; (B) global shift calculation; (C) peak list annotation and intensity-dependent shift calculation; (D) internal standard (IS)-specific shift analysis; (E) sample-level target screening; and (F) quantification. Input data includes centroided .mzML or Thermo .raw files, processed using rawrr (v1.2.0) and RaMS (v1.3.0). EICs are generated per m/z of interest, smoothed only for shape-dependent functions (not for quantification), and integrated via the trapezoidal rule. Peak shapes are encoded as Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAX) sequences (using seewave v2.2.0) with user-selectable alphabet size. Baseline is determined using the 25th intensity quantile by default, but elevated quantiles (up to 80th) are applied when EICs exhibit high noise—triggered by thresholds: (A) <25% zigzag pattern (alternating high/baseline intensities), (B) root mean squared error of background <10%, and (C) max intensity / 25th quantile >3. In-sample LOD and LOQ are defined as baseline + 3×noise and baseline + 10×noise, respectively. Peak identification uses a local maxima algorithm with customizable parameters: intensity_factor_decrease (>40%), intensity_factor_increase (>40%), density_factor (5× data density), and data density defined as points per 0.1 min. Peak splitting at likely cutoffs (edges of adjacent maxima) is enforced. Global shift (Function B) is calculated from all internal standards across samples, assuming the mean shift represents system-wide retention time drift; the largest observed shift defines the initial screening window (≥0.5 min for LC, ≥0.1 min for GC). Function C generates consensus peaks per reference standard, incorporates confirming ions for validation, and detects intensity-dependent shifts via linear regression of intensity vs. theoretical concentration—requiring inclusion of IS-only samples to identify unspecific interferences. Function D computes per-sample IS shifts to infer analyte-specific drifts, with fallback to uncorrected expected retention time if a valid peak is found precisely at that time. Function E performs target screening using adjusted windows incorporating global, intensity-dependent, and IS-dependent shifts; confirming ions are checked separately with ±20% intensity ratio tolerance; peaks failing shape similarity (via MINDIST on SAX sequences), minimal data points (≤7), or confirming ion detection are tagged 'CHECK'. Function F handles quantification: solvent blanks are used to estimate and subtract background (mean blank response); matrix-matched standards enable matrix correction; reference standards are outlier-checked via interquartile range (IQR); calibration uses six linear regression variants (through origin or unconstrained, with/without weighting by x or 1/x) optimized autonomously for R² ≥0.95 and median quantification error <30%, with high-leverage points iteratively removed using Cook’s distance until improvement ceases (minimum 4 points retained); final model selection prioritizes lowest quantification error, then widest concentration coverage, then highest R². Outputs include sample responses, response ratios, quantified concentrations, consensus peak lists, apex retention times, and qualitative heatmaps (TRUE/FALSE/masked)."}

Technical replicates were included across all data sets (e.g., triplicates for PIPMix and SpikeIn; two replicates per mixing ratio in ProteomeMix).', 'OpenMS_configuration_description': '', 'process_procedure_description': "FLASHQuant is a software tool for intact proteoform quantification from centroided LC-MS1 data, consisting of two main stages: feature group detection and quantity calculation. In the feature group detection stage, m/z traces (individual ion chromatograms) are first extracted from LC-MS spectra using MassTraceExtractor — a self-consistent kernel density estimator that connects peaks within instrument-specific mass accuracy tolerance along retention time; this extraction is performed before deconvolution to reduce noise and uses sliding-window binning of total retention time. Extracted m/z traces are then deconvolved per window and assembled into feature groups (representing putative proteoforms and their isotopes) using FLASHDeconv, which applies both charge and isotope deconvolution to assign monoisotopic masses. During this step, m/z traces may be assigned to multiple feature groups, resulting in 'shared' (overlapping) traces. In the quantity calculation stage, FLASHQuant resolves shared m/z traces via conflict resolution: for each shared trace, theoretical elution profiles (shapes) are estimated for its conflicting feature groups using only their non-shared m/z traces fitted to an exponential-Gaussian hybrid (EGH) function; the contribution of each theoretical shape to the shared trace is then estimated via non-negative least-squares optimization, enabling proportional distribution of the shared trace’s abundance among the corresponding feature groups. Finally, feature group abundance is calculated as the summed area under all constituent m/z trace curves. FLASHQuant outputs results in TSV format, including monoisotopic mass, retention time range, charge range, and quantity for each feature group. Additionally, the ConsensusFeatureGroupDetector tool is provided to identify feature groups consistently detected across multiple LC-MS runs (e.g., technical replicates) using user-defined mass and retention time tolerances (default: 20 ppm mass, 8 min RT), and supports input from other quantification tools (e.g., TopFD) when column names for mass, apex RT, and quantity are specified. Parameters used in benchmarking included those from ProSightPD (100 ppm mass tolerance, 8 min RT tolerance for consensus detection), and all runtime and performance comparisons were conducted on a desktop PC with Intel(R) Core(TM) i9–7900X CPU @ 3.30 GHz and 64 GB RAM."}

(iii) 'Machine Learning (Strategy 2)': Internal and external IDs were passed separately to FFId; RT windows for assay generation were widened to accommodate external RT uncertainty; OpenSWATH generated ~15 quality scores per feature candidate (including a custom RT deviation score); positive/negative training instances were selected based on internal ID matches (intensity-balanced sampling); LIBSVM (v3.12, RBF kernel) was trained via grid-search cross-validation (optimizing C and γ) after 0–1 scaling and sparse formatting; SVM probabilities were used to select features for external-only assays, while internal-assay features retained ID-based selection; FDR estimation was performed by comparing SVM-selected vs. gold-standard features and scaling by fraction of external-only assays. (3) Downstream analysis: Peptide-level CVs were computed in R (v3.3.0/3.3.2) after normalization to equal medians, summing modified variants, and filtering to peptides quantified in all 12 runs; protein quantification used MSstats (v3.6.0) with 'dataProcess' (top 10 features), 'quantification', and 'groupComparison' functions on ProteinQuantifier-exported, charge-filtered, and missing-value–filtered data."}

PCA is applied to the gene expression matrix Y = [y₁, y₂, ..., y_T] ∈ ℝ^(l×T), where l is the number of genes and T is the number of time points. Each gene i corresponds to a vector g_i ∈ ℝ^T (the i-th row of Y), and the set {g_i} forms a linear space. PCA is performed on the covariance matrix of these g_i vectors. The number of hidden variables m is determined as the smallest integer satisfying ∑_{k=m+1}^{min(l,T)} λ_k / ∑_{k=1}^{min(l,T)} λ_k ≤ 20%, where λ_k are the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix sorted in descending order. Pairwise correlations between tear trace elements and dry eye parameters were visualized using heatmap illustrations. Weighted Quantile Sum (WQS) regression was applied to identify the highest-contributing trace element for each dry eye parameter. Conditioned responses (CRs) were identified in CS-only trials if: (1) maximum eyelid closure amplitude >0.05 between 100–500 ms post-CS onset, and (2) positive slope in the 150-ms window before expected US delivery time. CR percentage (proportion of CRs per session), eye closure amplitude (all trials and CR-only trials), latency to CR onset (only in non-startle trials), and latency to CR peak were computed. Startle trials were identified by detecting peaks in the first derivative (velocity signal) of eyelid position occurring 30–80 ms post-CS onset, exceeding both 3 SDs of the 500-ms pre-CS baseline and an arbitrary threshold of 0.00025. Key methodological standardizations included: (a) separation of classification and explicit selection steps — all original explicit selection rules (e.g., minimal saccade amplitude A_min, minimal fixation duration T_min) were removed from the core algorithms and applied uniformly post-classification; (b) removal of interpolation for handling NaN-valued data holes — instead, holes were explicitly encoded: for fixation pickers, a hole within a fixation triggered splitting (end-of-hole marked as fixation start, start-of-hole as fixation end); for saccade pickers, holes were treated as saccade candidates; (c) removal of built-in merge rules — merging occurred implicitly when small saccades or holes were deselected, thereby joining adjacent fixation candidates; (d) unit standardization — all parameters converted to biophysically meaningful units: degrees (°) for angular position/amplitude, degrees/second (°/s) for velocity thresholds, and milliseconds (ms) for time-related parameters (e.g., window durations); (e) velocity filter harmonization — symmetrical moving-window velocity filters used with fixed temporal durations: 21 ms (10+1+10 samples) for EL1000+ data and 20 ms (2+1+2 samples) for both SMI data sets; (f) algorithm categorization into saccade pickers (I2MW, NH2010) and fixation pickers (CDT, HC2013, I2MC, KF, MST), each processed via distinct pipelines (Fig. 2): for fixation pickers, inter-fixation intervals were operationalized as saccade candidates and filtered using two sequential selection rules — first, removal of saccade candidates with amplitude < A_min (with T_min coupled to A_min via T_min = 2.2 × A_min + 27), thereby merging adjacent fixations; second, removal of fixation candidates with duration < T_min; for saccade pickers, fixation candidates were defined as inter-saccade intervals augmented with trial boundaries and hole boundaries, followed by identical two-stage selection. Four parameter combinations were tested: (A_min = 0.0°, T_min = 0 ms), (A_min = 0.3°, T_min = 0 ms), (A_min = 1.0°, T_min = 0 ms), and (A_min = 1.0°, T_min = 60 ms). Fixation agreement across algorithms was quantified using Hooge et al. (2018)’s event-based F1-score, computed before and after merging and selection.'}

Saccades were identified based on instantaneous velocity computed from a three-point moving average of x- and y-eye positions (in degrees); a saccade was labeled when velocity exceeded 2 standard deviations above the mean fixation velocity (<50°/s) for at least five consecutive points. Saccade reaction time (SRT) was defined as the time from peripheral target appearance to primary saccade onset. Saccades were classified as predictive (SRT < 90 ms), express (90–120 ms), or regular (>120 ms) based on established neurophysiological criteria and validated by bimodality coefficient analysis (BC = 0.63 for metronome, 0.54 for random task) of SRT distributions >90 ms. For saccade metrics, peak velocity and amplitude were analyzed; saccades with peak velocity >1000°/s were excluded (0.23% of total saccades). The main sequence was modeled using a square-root function (y = V√x) per saccade type (predictive, express, regular), fitted at both group and individual subject levels. Pupil size was analyzed in 2-ms bins, averaged over a 200-ms epoch following saccade end (provided ≥200-ms post-saccadic fixation was maintained), excluding trials with blinks, saccades, fixation onset delays >100 ms, or pupil velocity outside −5000 to 5000°/s. Blink metrics were extracted by detecting loss of eye-tracking signal consistent with literature-defined blink durations (50–300 ms); blink rate was computed as blinks per minute per trial, and blink timing relative to target appearance was analyzed in three epochs (−1000–1000 ms, −1000–0 ms, 0–+1000 ms), further stratified by saccade type. Each trial began with a 1000 ms fixation cross ('+'), followed by a stream of 10 stimuli presented at 1 stimulus per 90 ms (15 ms stimulus duration + 75 ms inter-stimulus interval). atom features (element type, number of bound hydrogens, ring membership) and bond features (bond type, ring membership) are encoded as integers and embedded into 300-dimensional vectors via learnable embedding layers; (2) Graph neural network processing: A 6-layer Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN) is applied by default (though GCN, RGCN, GAT, and Graph Transformer layers are supported), with Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation after each layer; node representations are updated via message-passing: h_i = ϕ(x_i, ⊕_{j∈N_i} ψ(x_i, x_j)), where ⊕ is summation aggregation and ϕ/ψ are learnable functions; (3) Prediction head computation: For fragment ion abundance θ_f, edge features are constructed by concatenating embeddings of the two incident atoms, the edge embedding, and covariates (molecular weight, precursor ion mode ([M+H]+/[M−H]−), collision energy, instrument type), then passed through a two-layer fully connected network outputting a 10-dimensional logit vector (5 ion modes × 2 fragment sides per edge break); precursor stability σ is computed from the global mean-pooled graph embedding concatenated with the same covariates, processed by two fully connected layers yielding a scalar logit; all logits (σ and θ_f for all f ∈ F(G)) are jointly normalized via softmax to produce fragment and precursor probabilities p(f); (4) Spectrum reconstruction and post-processing: Predicted subgraphs (fragments) are traced back using the edge map; exact m/z values are reconstructed from fragment mass and hydrogen loss count (0–3 H); peak intensities are obtained by summing probabilities of all fragment ions falling within the m/z tolerance window (50 ppm for NIST/MS-DIAL, 10 ppm for MSnLib); RT and CCS values are predicted separately using the same mean-pooled graph embedding fed into dedicated dense layers (frozen during fragment training) with standard MSE loss; training uses weighted mean squared error loss between predicted fragment probabilities and observed probabilities (derived from square-root-transformed peak intensities matched to F(G)), weighted by 1/(number of spectra per compound) to mitigate compound-level bias; optimization employs ADAM with learning rate scheduling on validation loss plateau over 200 epochs; ICEBERG was trained identically to FIORA (same splits, same workflow) using the GitHub repository (commit from Oct 21, 2023); all software dependencies rely on PyTorch Geometric for GNN implementation.'}

First, experimental MS2 spectra were exported from Agilent .d files into MGF format. The Python script then performed formatting standardization and de-duplication: for each unique precursor m/z, only the MS2 spectrum with the highest sum intensity of fragment ions was retained. Next, for each experimental spectrum, candidate compounds were retrieved from the CFM-ID database based on 10-ppm mass match (and optionally formula match). Three scoring approaches were evaluated: (1) '1:1 matching' — only the CFM-ID spectrum at the same CE level as the experimental spectrum was scored; (2) '1:3 summation' — scores from all three CFM-ID CE levels (10, 20, 40 V) were summed for a given experimental spectrum; (3) '9-way summation' — scores from all nine combinations of experimental CE (10/20/40 V) × in silico CE (10/20/40 V) were summed. All scoring used the dot-product algorithm with 0.02 Da fragment tolerance. For each experimental spectrum, resulting scores were used to rank candidate compounds, compute percentile ranks (relative position among all candidates), and quotient values (candidate score divided by maximum candidate score for that spectrum). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed globally across all 845 'pass' compounds to determine optimal cutoff thresholds (percentile and quotient) achieving ≥0.90 true positive rate (TPR); these global thresholds were then applied mixture-wise to compute mixture-specific TPRs and false positive rates (FPRs) as performance metrics. Analyses were conducted both with and without formula filtering to assess robustness under realistic (mass-only) versus idealized (formula-known) conditions."}

OneMod comprises two main stages: (1) SpXMod—a generalized linear modelling tool implementing stage-wise regression with correlated, dimension-specific intercepts and covariate coefficients—using five covariates: Socio-demographic Index (SDI), HIV mortality rate (zero before 1981), age-standardized COVID-19 mortality rate (zero before 2020), island binary indicator, and an all-risk-factor summary covariate (population attributable fraction for all risk factors combined, available only from 1990 onward). SpXMod operates in four stages: stage 1 fits a global age-specific covariate model with age- and location-specific intercepts; stage 2 uses those results as an offset to fit super-region- and age-specific trends and intercepts; stage 3 adds country-specific and age-specific intercepts; and stage 4 (for subnational locations) adds subnational intercepts. A custom splicing step combines models fitted for 1950–onward and 1990–onward datasets. (2) KReg—a Kronecker-factored multivariate kernel regression model—applies non-parametric smoothing to SpXMod residuals across age, time, and location dimensions using kernel methods, starting from the parametric fit and leveraging correlations encoded in the overall likelihood. Binomial likelihood is used throughout. Preprocessing includes compactification techniques to ensure binomial parameters remain <1 (especially for neonatal and oldest age groups) and weight adjustments to account for non-sampling variation. Uncertainty propagation uses 1000 Monte Carlo draws per location-year-sex combination; calibration ensures scaled Pearson residuals have unit variance at chosen geographical granularity. Final outputs include single-year-age life tables incorporating fatal discontinuities (sex- and age-redistributed by cause), abridged life tables for standard GBD age groups, life expectancy at birth, and final mortality envelopes. Software used includes Python (v3.10.4), Stata (v15.1), and R (v4.2 and v4.4); code is publicly available. Expected SDI-based mortality was estimated separately using MR-BRT (meta-regression–Bayesian, regularised, trimmed) with cubic B-splines (five knots between 0–1, enforced linearity at extremes) and an ensemble of >50 randomly knot-placed models per age-sex group.'}

{'sample_description': "The sample used in the research consists of 9,559 unique chemical compounds from the U.S. EPA’s ToxCast program and NIH Tox21 initiative, as compiled in the invitroDBv4.1 MySQL database. After rigorous structural curation—including removal of duplicates, unspecified organic/inorganic molecules, and entries lacking DTXSID or valid SMILES; standardization via RDKit (e.g., hydrogen removal, ring aromatization, tautomer normalization, charge/metal/stereoisomer/counter-ion removal); and fingerprint generation—the final dataset comprised 9,358 chemically well-defined compounds. Structural representations were converted into five types of molecular fingerprints: FP3 (55 bits), FP4 (307 bits), MACCS (166 bits), PubChem (881 bits), and Klekota-Roth (4,860 bits), resulting in a unified feature matrix of n = 1,797 binary bits cross-referenced with SIRIUS fingerprint definitions (positive mode, 3,877-bit subset). The MassBank database (release 2024.06, 117,732 spectra, including 2,879 Eawag-submitted spectra since 2022) was used to define compound-specific validation sets: compounds present in MassBank were assigned to the corresponding assay’s MassBank validation set, while the remaining compounds formed the training and internal test splits.", 'SIRIUS_configuration_description': 'SIRIUS was not directly executed or configured in this study; rather, its fingerprint definition system was used as a reference standard for selecting and aligning molecular fingerprints. Specifically, the 1,797-bit feature vector used in ML modeling was constructed by cross-referencing generated fingerprints (FP3, FP4, MACCS, PubChem, Klekota-Roth) with the SIRIUS fingerprint definitions for the positive mode (3,877 bits total), excluding extended connectivity fingerprints (ECFP), custom SMARTS patterns, and ring systems — as these were deemed computationally challenging and showed no significant improvement in predictive power during proof-of-concept testing. No SIRIUS software parameters (e.g., mass accuracy tolerance, isotope pattern scoring, CSI:FingerID settings, or fragmentation tree computation options) were applied, modified, or reported, because SIRIUS itself was not employed for spectral analysis, structure identification, or molecular formula prediction; it served solely as a curated bit-index reference for fingerprint bit naming and alignment in the MLinvitroTox pipeline.', 'process_procedure_description': "The process procedure involved a multi-stage computational pipeline centered on pytcpl — a custom Python package developed for preprocessing invitroDBv4.1 bioactivity data — integrated with RDKit, Pybel (Open Babel), and CDK-pywrapper for cheminformatics operations, and downstream machine learning using MLinvitroTox. Key steps included: (1) Outlier removal: For each concentration-response series, a smoothed response curve was computed via running mean across neighboring concentrations; residuals were calculated, and points flagged as outliers if (i) residual > baseline median absolute deviation (BMAD, computed from three lowest concentrations) AND (ii) residual > 5 × standard deviation of residuals. (2) Curve validation: Series required ≥4 tested concentrations and at least one median response > 0.8 × ACC (activity concentration at cutoff, defined per assay as 3×BMAD); failing concentration count → hitcall = NaN; failing response threshold → hitcall = 0. (3) Curve fitting: Four primary models were fit via maximum likelihood estimation — 'constant' (R(d)=0), 'hill' (3-parameter sigmoidal: R(d) = t / [1 + (g·d)^p]), 'gnls' (5-parameter gain-loss: R(d) = t·[1+(g·d)^p]/[1+(d/l)^q]), and 'forced hill' (applied when 'gnls' won: high-concentration points above 'gnls' top removed, then 'hill' refit). Additional models ('poly1', 'poly2', 'power', 'exp2', 'exp4', 'exp5', 'gnls2') were used only in bootstrapping. (4) Hitcall assignment: Winning model selected by lowest AIC; if 'constant', hitcall = 0; otherwise, continuous hitcall P_hit = P₁ × P₂ × P₃, where P₁ = probability ≥1 median response > ACC (via Student’s t-distribution), P₂ = probability curve top > ACC (likelihood ratio), P₃ = exp(−0.5·AIC_winning) / [exp(−0.5·AIC_winning) + exp(−0.5·AIC_constant)]. (5) Cytotoxicity correction: Final continuous hitcall P_hit_tgt = P_hit × (1 − P_cytotox), where P_cytotox = Φ[(ACC_cytotox − ACC_tgt) / √(SD_cytotox² + SD_tgt²)], with SD_ACC estimated as 0.41×ACC + 7.0 from bootstrapping; ACC_cytotox derived either from matched viability assays (fitted with 'forced hill') or cytotoxicity burst assays (median ACC across burst endpoints, weighted by n_hit/n_tested). (6) Bootstrapping: 300 bootstraps for 'All models' scenario (all tcplv3.0 models except 'exp3') and 1,000 for 'Forced hill' scenario (only 'constant', 'gnls', 'hill' + forced refit), using non-smoothed resampling with BMAD-level noise injection on 6,436 curves across 62 endpoints (~100 chemicals/endpoint). (7) Structural processing: RDKit standardized structures; Pybel (Open Babel) generated FP3 (55-bit) and FP4 (307-bit); CDK-pywrapper generated MACCS (166-bit), PubChem (881-bit), and Klekota-Roth (4,860-bit); all merged and aligned to SIRIUS positive-mode bit indices (3,877 bits), yielding final 1,797-bit fingerprint matrix. (8) ML data preparation: Continuous hitcalls linked to DTXSID and fingerprints; endpoints filtered to 490 based on activity/input thresholds and cHTS curation flags ('QC-omit', 'Flag-omit'); MassBank compounds (2024.06 release, 117,732 spectra, 2,879 Eawag spectra) assigned to assay-specific validation sets. All pytcpl and fingerprint generation scripts are publicly released as part of the MLinvitroTox package."}

For 900-ms SOA, 300 trials were presented (first 150 artifact-free epochs used); for 1800-ms and 3600-ms SOAs, 150 trials each were presented. Participants sat comfortably in a sound-attenuated room, wore binaural earphones, watched muted videos, and were instructed to ignore sounds and minimize movement; parents assisted when needed. EEG was recorded using the NeuroTravel system with 28 scalp electrodes placed per the 10–20 system (Fp1, Fp2, F3, Fz, F4, F7, F8, Fc3, Fcz, Fc4, C3, Cz, C4, Cp3, Cpz, Cp4, P3, Pz, P4, Tp7, Tp8, T3, T4, T5, T6, O1, Oz, O2), referenced to linked earlobes, grounded at AFz, with online filtering (0.01–70 Hz) and sampling at 500 Hz; electrode impedances were maintained below 10 kΩ. Bad channel interpolation was performed for 0–2 channels per participant. Artifact rejection involved automatic raw data inspection (±400 μV threshold), followed by independent component analysis (ICA) using the ALICE platform to remove eye movement and muscle artifacts. Data were epoched from −200 ms pre-stimulus to +500 ms post-stimulus, with additional automatic rejection of segments exceeding ±100 μV. ERPs were baseline-corrected to the −200 ms prestimulus interval. FCz electrode was selected for primary analysis due to robust auditory cortical response and reduced artifact susceptibility. ERP components (P1: 33–99 ms, N1: 96–173 ms, P2: 139–264 ms, N2: 210–365 ms) were identified by two blinded experts; only RS participants with evident morphology (n = 12) were retained for latency/amplitude quantification. Peak amplitudes were measured relative to baseline; latencies were measured from stimulus onset; peak-to-peak amplitudes (N1P1, P2N1, N2P2) were computed as amplitude differences between successive peaks to minimize contamination effects. Statistical analysis employed mixed ANOVA in R-Studio with Group (RS vs TD) as between-subjects factor, SOA (3 levels) as within-subjects factor, Age as covariate, and their interactions; estimation statistics used the Dabestr package; Pearson and partial Pearson correlations (controlling for age) were computed using the ppcor library in R; significance threshold was α = 0.05.'}

(9) RT prediction: QSRR model built using random forest (R package randomForest); 346 molecular descriptors (MDs) calculated via rcdk from SMILES (obtained from PubChem); MD filtering: remove MDs with >50% missing values, impute remaining missing values via KNN (R package impute), remove invariant MDs; optimized MD subsets selected based on RF importance (>50 appearances in top-5 across 100 models) separately for HILIC and RP separations.', 'process_procedure_description': 'The MetDNA workflow comprises six core sequential and recursive procedures: (1) Data import: MS1 peak table (.csv) and MS2 files (.mgf or .msp) are loaded; .mgf files are generated via ProteoWizard v3.0.6150; .msp files from MS-DIAL DIA processing bypass MS1–MS2 matching. (2) Initial seed metabolite annotation: MS1 peaks matched to MS2 spectra (±25 ppm, ±10 s); top-abundant MS2 selected per peak; matched pairs searched against in-house standard spectral library using modified DP scoring (Eq. 1); DP ≥0.8 in forward/reverse match retained; filtered by theoretical RT (±30%); resulting 50–200 high-confidence annotations become round-0 seed metabolites. (3) Isotope and adduct annotation: for each seed, theoretical isotope peaks ([M]–[M+4]) and adducts (from Supplementary Table 5) are calculated and matched to MS1 peaks using respective tolerances and scoring functions (Eqs. 2–6); isotope annotation of adducts follows identically. (4) MRN-based recursive neighbor annotation: seed metabolites mapped to the metabolic reaction network (MRN, 6439 nodes, 9603 edges, built from KEGG RPAIR/COMPOUND databases downloaded 7 March 2017 via KEGGREST); neighbor metabolites retrieved at reaction steps 1–3; surrogate MS2 spectra assigned; theoretical m/z (for adducts) and predicted RTs (via QSRR model) generated; experimental MS1 (±25 ppm), RT (±30%), and MS2 (dot-product ≥0.5) matched; Score_iden (Eq. 7) computed and used for ranking; isotope annotation repeated for newly annotated neighbors. (5) Recursive seed selection and iteration: newly annotated neighbor metabolites become seeds for next round; process repeats until no new seeds emerge. (6) Confidence assignment and redundancy removal: peaks grouped by annotation and RT (3 s window) into peak groups; grades assigned (1–4); recursive redundancy resolution prioritizes higher-grade annotations—first removing grade-4 annotations when higher-grade alternatives exist, then reassigning grades and repeating until redundancy stabilizes; final outputs include pathway enrichment (hypergeometric test on KEGG pathways), quantitative pathway expression (Pareto-scaled intensities averaged per pathway), and RT prediction (QSRR random forest trained on experimentally RT-annotated metabolites using optimized MD subsets for HILIC/RP).'}

(2) Metadata Harmonization: A Python workflow automates integration of NMDR (mwTAB) and MTBLS (ISA-Tab) metadata into ReDU’s ontology. {'sample_description': 'The study used three types of biological samples: (i) 22 human urine samples, (ii) 19 beer samples, and (iii) fecal (stool) samples. All samples were analyzed via LC–MS/MS using HILIC chromatography and Orbitrap-based detection.', 'MS2LDA_configuration_description': 'The MS2LDA+ model is an extension of standard Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) designed for mass spectrometry fragmentation data, where a single shared set of Mass2Motifs (topics) is inferred across multiple samples. It employs a Variational Bayes inference scheme in which each sample is modeled with standard MS2LDA, but motif updates are pooled across all samples. The model outputs Mass2Motifs (collections of co-occurring fragment ions and neutral losses) and per-sample prevalence vectors α_f, where each element α_k^f represents the proportion of total feature intensity in sample f explained by Mass2Motif k. The implementation includes two complementary linking scores: (1) Mass2Motif–molecule probability (proportion of a molecule’s spectrum explained by the Mass2Motif), and (2) overlap score (proportion of the Mass2Motif present in the molecule’s spectrum, i.e., how many Mass2Motif fragments/losses are observed). The model enforces that every MS2 spectrum is assigned to at least one Mass2Motif. The software implementation is available on GitHub (https://github.com/sdrogers/lda); no specific version or command-line parameters are stated, but inference details are described in Supporting Information section S4.
